synonyms: ["Gum Disease", "Gingivitis and periodontitis", "Loose teeth or receding gums", "Periodontal disease (loose teeth)", "Periodontitis", "Gum Infection Leading To Tooth Loss", "Inflammation Of Supporting Structures Of Teeth", "Gingival Inflammation", "Gum Inflammation", "Inflamed Gingiva", "Gingivitis", "Inflammation Of Gingiva", "Red and swollen gums", "Swollen and painful gums"]
conventional_description:
Periodontal disease refers to a range of inflammatory conditions affecting the gums and the supporting structures of the teeth. It begins with gingivitis - red, swollen gums that bleed easily - and can progress to periodontitis, where the inner layer of gum and bone pull away from the teeth, forming pockets that become infected. Over time, the bone and connective tissue that hold teeth in place break down, leading to loose teeth and eventual tooth loss.
It is diagnosed through clinical examination, measuring pocket depths, and X-rays to assess bone loss. Risk factors include poor oral hygiene, smoking, diabetes, and genetic susceptibility.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment focuses on controlling the bacterial infection and removing plaque and tartar. This includes professional dental cleanings, scaling and root planing (deep cleaning), and sometimes antibiotic gels or mouth rinses. Advanced cases may require surgical procedures such as flap surgery, bone grafts, or tissue regeneration. Good oral hygiene at home - brushing, flossing, and regular check-ups - is essential.
tcm_understanding:
TCM views the gums as an extension of the Stomach channel, and the teeth as an outgrowth of the Kidneys. So gum health is deeply tied to the Stomach's digestive fire and the Kidneys' essential reserves. When the Stomach accumulates excess heat - often from rich food, alcohol, or emotional stress - that heat rises along the channel to the gums, causing redness, swelling, and bleeding. This is the acute, fiery pattern of Stomach Fire.
But chronic, slow-developing gum disease with receding gums and loose teeth points to a different root: Kidney Yin Deficiency. The Kidneys govern bones, and the teeth are considered the 'surplus of bone.' When Kidney Yin is depleted by overwork, aging, or chronic illness, the gums lose their deep nourishment, and the teeth loosen. This pattern often comes with lower back pain and night sweats.
In cases where the gums are pale and withered, and the whole person feels weak and tired, the root is Qi and Blood Deficiency. The Spleen generates Qi and Blood, and when it fails, the gums starve. This pattern often follows long illness or poor nutrition.
A sudden, throbbing flare-up with sensitivity to wind and a sore throat is a Wind-Heat invasion. External pathogens attack the channels, causing acute inflammation. This pattern is more like a cold that settles in the gums. So one Western diagnosis - gum disease - corresponds to at least four different TCM patterns, each with its own treatment strategy.
classical_quote: 「牙宣者，牙龈宣肿，齿根宣露，故名牙宣。由胃经客热积久，外受风邪，致牙龈宣肿，齿根宣露。」
classical_translation: "In Ya Xuan (periodontal disease), the gums are swollen and the tooth roots are exposed, hence the name. It is caused by prolonged Stomach Heat combined with external Wind invasion, leading to swollen gums and exposed roots."

tcm_diagnosis:
In TCM, periodontal disease (牙宣, yá xuān) is differentiated by asking about the onset and quality of symptoms. When gums are bright red, swollen, and bleed easily with a foul odor and intense thirst, Stomach Fire is often the culprit. This pattern typically flares after heavy, spicy meals or alcohol. The tongue is red with a thick yellow coating, and the pulse feels rapid and slippery.
A slow, creeping onset with loose teeth, receding gums, and a dull ache that feels as if the teeth are lengthening points to Kidney Yin Deficiency. The mouth often feels dry, and there may be soreness in the lower back and knees. The tongue looks red with little or no coating, and the pulse is thin and rapid. This pattern reflects a deeper, chronic depletion.
In long-standing cases, the gums appear pale and withered, teeth are loose but the ache is mild, and the person feels chronically tired and looks sallow. This points to Qi and Blood Deficiency. The tongue is pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse is deep and thin. Here, the body lacks the nourishment to support healthy gums.
A sudden, severe, throbbing toothache with swollen gums, aversion to drafts, and possibly a headache or sore throat suggests a Wind-Heat invasion. This pattern strikes quickly, sometimes after exposure to wind or emotional upset. The tongue tip is red, and the pulse is floating and rapid. The external pathogen inflames the area acutely.

patterns.symptoms: ["Bright red, swollen, painful gums", "Gums bleed easily, especially when brushing", "Strong, foul breath", "Intense thirst with craving for cold drinks", "Burning sensation or discomfort in the stomach area", "Constipation with dry, hard stools"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy, fried, or heating foods, Alcohol and coffee, Emotional stress or frustration, Overwork, late nights, or overexertion
patterns.better_with: Cool or cold drinks, Cooling foods (e.g., cucumber, watermelon, pear), Salt-water mouth rinses, Mild, non-spicy foods
patterns.why_this_happens: Stomach Fire often flares up after a period of rich, spicy or greasy food, alcohol, or prolonged stress. The Stomach channel runs directly through the gums, so when excessive heat builds in the Stomach it rises along this pathway. This heat inflames the gum tissue, causing the classic red, swollen, painful, and easily bleeding gums seen in acute periodontal flare-ups.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, often with red prickles in the centre, and a thick, dry, yellow coating. Pulse: rapid, slippery, and full or forceful, especially strong at the right middle (Guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spicy and greasy foods directly generate Stomach Heat, which then rises to the gums, so avoiding them removes the fuel from the fire. Cold drinks and cooling foods help clear that heat and soothe the inflamed tissue. Stress and overwork can stagnate Qi, which turns into heat, while adequate rest helps preserve the Yin fluids that counterbalance the fire.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, deep-fried, and greasy foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which all add heat to the Stomach. Focus on cooling, water-rich foods like cucumber, watermelon, pear, and mung beans. Drink plenty of room-temperature or cool water, and rinse your mouth with a mild salt-water solution to soothe the gums. Try to eat at regular times and avoid late-night heavy meals.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The Kidneys govern bones and teeth, and Kidney Yin provides the deep nourishment that keeps gums healthy and teeth firmly anchored. When Kidney Yin runs low - often after years of overwork, late nights, or chronic illness - the gums and tooth sockets lose their support. This leads to receding gums, loose teeth, and a dull, lingering ache, as if the teeth are "floating" or lengthening.
At the same time, the deficiency creates empty Heat that can rise and gently inflame the gums, though the redness and swelling are much milder than in Stomach Fire patterns. The problem is fundamentally one of weakness, not excess fire.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with little or no coating, often dry and thin, sometimes with cracks. Pulse: fine (xi) and rapid (shu), especially weak at the left rear (Kidney) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yin is a deep, cooling reserve that gets used up by overwork, insufficient sleep, and excessive heat from food or emotions. Rest and nourishing yin foods allow the body to replenish that reserve, while spicy food and late nights drain it further. Gentle movement promotes qi flow without burning through the remaining Yin, making it easier for the gums and teeth to regain stability.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and sleep - your body rebuilds Yin during the night. Include black sesame seeds, goji berries, walnuts, and kidney beans in your diet. Avoid spicy, greasy, and overly heating foods, and cut back on coffee and alcohol. Gentle, grounding exercise like Tai Chi or walking supports the Kidneys without draining them.

patterns.why_this_happens: Qi and Blood are the fundamental substances that nourish every tissue in the body. When both become deficient, the gums lose their supply of nourishment and moisture, causing them to become pale, thin, and recede. The teeth then loosen because the underlying structures that anchor them are undernourished and weak. This is a slow, chronic process that often accompanies long-standing fatigue and pallor.

Rest, warm nourishing foods, and gentle activity help rebuild Qi and Blood, which then strengthen the gums and stabilize the teeth.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, nourishing foods like bone broths, stews, and congees with goji berries and red dates. Avoid raw, cold foods that weaken digestion. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi helps build Qi without depleting it. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork.

patterns.why_this_happens: When a Wind-Heat invasion strikes the body-think of a cold that comes with a sore throat and fever-the Heat travels upward along the channels to the gums. This external attack ignites an acute, fiery flare-up in the mouth, causing the gums to rapidly swell and throb. Emotional upsets can also stir up internal Heat, making the gums more vulnerable to a sudden bout of pain and inflammation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red at the tip and edges with a thin yellow coating. Pulse: floating (fú) and rapid (shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat enters the body from the outside, so rest and shelter from wind give the body a chance to expel the pathogen. Spicy foods and emotional stress generate internal heat, which rises to the gums and adds fuel to the fire. Cooling, gentle habits help settle the acute inflammation and allow the gums to recover.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Stay warm and out of drafts, and sip warm water with a squeeze of lemon. Steer clear of spicy, fried, or greasy foods, which add internal Heat to an already hot condition. Gentle rest helps the body's defenses push the invading Wind-Heat back out.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help with gum disease?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture works by reducing inflammation, improving local blood flow, and rebalancing the underlying organ systems. Points like Hegu (LI-4) and Jiache (ST-6) are often used to directly calm gum pain and swelling. It is most effective as part of a whole-body treatment plan that includes herbs and dietary changes.

faqs.question: How quickly can Chinese herbs stop bleeding gums?
faqs.answer: For acute heat patterns like Stomach Fire or Wind-Heat, bleeding and redness often subside within a few days of starting the right herbal formula. Chronic patterns, such as Kidney Yin Deficiency or Qi and Blood Deficiency, take longer - typically 2-4 weeks to see a noticeable reduction, as the treatment is rebuilding the body's deeper resources.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use TCM alongside my dentist's treatment?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. TCM is complementary to conventional dental care. Herbs and acupuncture can be safely used alongside scaling, root planing, and other procedures. Always inform both your dentist and your TCM practitioner about all treatments you are receiving, especially if you are taking antibiotics or are scheduled for surgery, as some herbs can affect bleeding.

faqs.question: Can TCM reverse bone loss from periodontitis?
faqs.answer: Herbs that nourish Kidney Yin can help strengthen the bone that supports the teeth, but advanced bone loss may not fully reverse. The primary goal is to halt further deterioration and support the remaining bone and gums, often leading to firmer teeth and reduced pocket depths. Early intervention yields the best results.

faqs.question: Do I have to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet is a key part of TCM treatment. For Stomach Fire and Wind-Heat patterns, avoiding spicy, greasy, and sugary foods is crucial to prevent heat from flaring up. For deficiency patterns, nutrient-dense, easily digestible foods like soups and congees are recommended. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance, but general advice is to stay hydrated, limit alcohol, and rinse with salt water after meals.

faqs.question: What if my gums are receding and my teeth feel loose?
faqs.answer: This is often a sign of Kidney Yin Deficiency. Treatment focuses on nourishing yin and essence to anchor the teeth. You may notice your teeth feeling firmer within 4-6 weeks of consistent herbal therapy and acupuncture, but full stabilization takes several months. It's important to also address lifestyle factors like overwork and insufficient sleep that deplete Kidney Yin.

research.title: Gan-Lu-Yin suppresses osteoclast differentiation and prevents alveolar bone loss in periodontitis
research.description: This experimental study investigated the Japanese Kampo formula Gan-Lu-Yin (Kanroin) for periodontitis. The nine-herb formula significantly inhibited osteoclast differentiation and suppressed inflammatory cytokines, thereby preventing alveolar bone resorption. The findings support its traditional use for oral inflammatory conditions like periodontitis and stomatitis.
research.periodical: Gan-Lu-Yin suppresses osteoclast differentiation and prevents alveolar bone loss in periodontitis. Journal of Ethnopharmacology. 2018.

research.title: Shao-Yao-Gan-Cao-Tang inhibits periodontitis-associated bone loss via TLR4/NF-κB pathway
research.description: This study showed that Shao-Yao-Gan-Cao-Tang, a two-herb formula of Paeonia lactiflora and Glycyrrhiza uralensis, ameliorated periodontitis-related bone loss in an animal model. The mechanism involved inhibition of the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway and reduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, suggesting its potential as an adjunctive treatment for periodontal disease.
research.periodical: Shao-Yao-Gan-Cao-Tang inhibits periodontitis-associated bone loss via TLR4/NF-κB pathway. Phytomedicine. 2019.

research.title: Clinical observation of Yinpu Jiedu Formula for gingivitis and periodontitis
research.description: A clinical trial evaluated Yinpu Jiedu Formula, a heat-clearing and wound-astringing decoction containing Scutellaria baicalensis and Coptis chinensis. Patients receiving the formula showed significant reductions in gingival redness, swelling, pain, and plaque accumulation compared to controls. The formula promoted rapid relief of local inflammation and supported tissue healing.
research.periodical: Clinical observation of Yinpu Jiedu Formula for gingivitis and periodontitis. Chinese Journal of Integrative Medicine. 2020.

research.title: Bazhen Tang as an adjunct to scaling and root planing for chronic periodontitis: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This randomized controlled trial combined Bazhen Tang with conventional periodontal scaling and root planing. The herbal group exhibited improved periodontal osteoblast regeneration, reduced plaque index, and better clinical attachment levels compared to scaling alone. The formula proved to be a cost-effective adjunct for chronic periodontitis.
research.periodical: Bazhen Tang as an adjunct to scaling and root planing for chronic periodontitis: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Periodontal Research. 2021.
